utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and those who are assisting us just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Edgerton, are you ready to continue the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. If I could just have a moment of your time to address you on a scheduling matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we do that. I'm advised by my colleagues and our staff that the next witness who is scheduled to testify here was only able to arrive here in the country and here in The Hague late last night. She'd had some eye surgery that had prevented her from travelling any earlier and while she has arrived, I understand she's only being proofed at this moment. We've advised Ms. Loukas of this and in my submission, Your Honour, I don't think should Your Honours agree that in the circumstances to allow for sufficient preparation of this witness who's also a victim of sexual assault, in my submission it wouldn't adversely affect our scheduling overall if we were to finish with this witness today and begin the next witness tomorrow morning, especially given her absolutely late arrival time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just prior to Your Honours coming on the Bench, Ms. Edgerton raised that issue with me and I certainly don't have a problem with commencing the witness tomorrow morning and ending today's proceedings once the current witness has finished giving her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, given these specific circumstances now, eye surgery you mentioned, the Chamber agrees; we will allow you to commence the next witness tomorrow morning. At the same time, I would like to make the observation that even if it would not disturb your scheduling on the short term, you should keep in mind, the OTP should keep in mind that it's not only this week and next week we are dealing with but we are also heading for concluding the Prosecution's case and of course in the long term, it could have some influence. And I want you to keep that clearly in mind. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- I might indicate that I have -- Mr. Karganovic is outside the court is in the Defence room attending to some matters but he will be coming into the courtroom in perhaps 10 to 15 minutes. Sometimes there seem to be problems with allowing people in after the session has started and I just wanted to ensure that there's no problem with Mr. Karganovic coming in after the session has begun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What would you like me to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour, I think I'm basically informing the Trial Chamber so that the people outside the courtroom can hear that and ensure that Mr. Karganovic has safe passage into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has no problem in Mr. Karganovic entering the courtroom when we have started. I don't know whether everyone is really listening in such detail, but perhaps Madam Registrar, you could inform security that there's no problem as far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness 84. May I first remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Before, Ms. Edgerton, I give you the opportunity to continue the examination, I'd like to consult the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- before we begin to make sure that we remain in private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Witness 84, I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to testify on matters that certainly were painful for you. We have observed that, and we perhaps therefore even more appreciate than on average that you came, that you answered the questions of the parties and of the Bench. I wish you all the best for the future, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you for showing great consideration for me and the fact that the Defence decided not to cross-examine me. Given what I have been through and what I have experienced, it is difficult to go back to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Usher, could you please escort Witness 84 out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might indicate now that the witness has gone, there are three matters I wish to place on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. It can be done in open session, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it should be done in open session. Firstly, Your Honour will note that I, of course, did not cross-examine the witness other than when Your Honour decided to ask more questions and certain issues arose as a result. But -- and I also understand the approach that Ms. Edgerton has adopted with the witness and I think it's also very important for the witness to be able to contribute to the process before the Court. But at the same time, Your Honour, when we are dealing with evidence of this nature, it's of a particular emotional overload for all concerned and it is in a situation where my client, Mr. Krajisnik, could not possibly be found under any heading of vicarious liability or otherwise guilty of opportunistic incidents of this nature; that, Your Honour, I put a marker there as to the nature and extent of the evidence being called by the Prosecution and I submit that Your Honour should give some guidance to the Prosecution generally in relation to these issues. I leave Ms. Edgerton out of this because ultimately she's not responsible for the Prosecution policy in relation to this case. But Your Honour often speaks of time constraints and it seems to me that a lot of the additional information was simply not germane to the issues that Your Honours are dealing with in this case and could not be germane. In those circumstances, Your Honour, I think it's appropriate for the Trial Chamber to give the Prosecution some guidance particularly in relation to matters of this nature. And as I indicated, I understand completely the approach that Ms. Edgerton has adopted with this particular witness and I understand particularly the witness's need to speak about her experiences. But at the same time, in relation to the issues that are before the Trial Chamber, some discretion and some balance must be reached particularly in circumstances where Your Honour is constantly talking about our problems with time. That's the first point I place on the table. The second point is this, Your Honour, and this is a matter I've raised ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, what do you have in mind? Do you have in mind irrelevant questions or do you have in mind questions concerning how matters developed in Grbavica in more general terms rather than specifically in relation to what happened to this witness in her direct contacts with the person she mentioned? It's not entirely clear whether you are -- I mean for example, let me say, are you talking about the relevance of the question where the bread came from, where the bakery was on the one side of the river or the other side or -- is it that kind of matters or is it about the witness staying in Grbavica for perhaps a relatively long period of time and experiencing on whether they were free to leave or -- it's not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well I think Your Honour gave a very fine example in that first aspect of the sort of thing that quite frankly does not assist the Trial Chamber and particularly in circumstances where Your Honour is quite intensely curtailing the time available to the Defence when we are questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are now repeating. But it's clear to me you say a lot of irrelevant stuff was asked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Absolute he Your Honour, and I think that's quite clear to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now that's the first point. The second point is this, Your Honour. Your Honour, I've placed on the record before and this is in relation to Your Honour's leading questions to witnesses. Now, I understand it's a hybrid system; I understand that we're dealing with a situation whereby in this hybrid that has been created here that Your Honours are a lot more interventionist with witnesses. But -- and I understand Your Honours consider that it is in only in exceptional circumstances that objection can be taken to leading questions from a Judge. But at the same time, Your Honour, and I've made this point before: Leading questions on critical areas, and particularly of the generalist nature that Your Honour offered to the witness in relation to uniforms, when Ms. Edgerton had painstakingly taken the witness through in detail in relation to uniforms and then to try to wrap up the question up in a leading way, in a generalised form about the nature of the uniforms, Your Honour, in a leading format, I would submit is not appropriate. That's the second matter I place on the record. Thirdly, Your Honour, on a number of occasions with the last two witnesses specifically, but prior to this as well -- this is 503 and 073 I'm talking about, not in relation to this witness because I didn't need to cross-examine to any real extent other than following upon Your Honour's leading questions. Now I'm entitled as an advocate, Your Honour, to secure my client's position in cross-examination by closing doors or closing gates, as Your Honour has referred to it and as I refer to it as well. As is implicit in that comment, Your Honour, in that description, that is seeking to ensure that the witness - and I'm not talking about the last witness, I'm talking about the two witnesses before that - cannot avoid the consequences of their answer by saying -- by coming up with "I was never asked about that," when it was quite clearly an area that he they would have been asked about, or "It must have been the translators" or "I didn't check." Now, Your Honour, unless Your Honour allows, and this is with the greatest of respect, Your Honour, the effect of what Your Honour is doing by precluding cross-examination by saying, "Look, this is just closing gates, we know where you're going Ms. Loukas and we are professional judges and we'll assess the escape route," what happens, Your Honour, in reality, is that Your Honour is providing witnesses with escape hatches that they accept with alacrity. And with the greatest of respect, Your Honour, I must place this on the record because this approach to cross-examination by Your Honour is contrary, in my submission, to procedural fairness and I implore Your Honour not to do it. And I place that very clearly on the record should this matter come to the appeal stage, firstly; and secondly, -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, if it's on the record, it's available to the Appeals Chamber. That needs no explanation. If there's anything else you'd like to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, those are the three points. Firstly in relation to the question of the last witness, and I dealt with that; second, in relation to Your Honour's leading questions to witnesses; and thirdly, in relation to this question of cross-examination. While Your Honour, we all have to adjust our approaches in terms of the hybrid between the civil law and the common law, we cannot end up with a situation whereby we take the worst of both systems and end up the protections of neither. And additionally, if one looks at overall in terms of the question of human rights, Your Honour, the human rights of the accused are part of what the court is here to protect, of course. And Your Honours are very well aware of that. But I need to place these things on the record because the leading questions from Your Honours and the interference with cross-examination and my submissions in relation to those matters must be placed on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. I'll not extensively comment on it. It's not my recollection that I put any question to the witness in relation to uniforms apart from when, in one of her answers, she referred to uniforms herself. That's one. The second issue is about relevant and irrelevant questions. The Chamber regretfully has to agree with you to some extent what the location of the bakery was, a specific question; whether two, three, or four guards would do a search; whether that was on weekends or during weekdays; what exactly the location of the building or certain building was, if there is no follow-up; what exactly the stove would be if there is no electricity. These are just examples of questions that really do not assist in any way, whether it's wood or whether it would be petrol in the stove. It was clear from the witness that it would be due to lack of electricity that they had to rely on other sources of heating. It's not dramatic but since Ms. Loukas raised the issue and since I did write a few examples for myself, I just bring it to the attention of the Office of the Prosecution. Finally, I have to apologise for not well reading, perhaps, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transcript of yesterday. I said this morning you were talking about four days giving statements. What you said, actually, I reread it, is that you said on three days in 1996 and two days in 1997 which I more favourably could have read as three days in 1996 and two days in 1997 and if I would have read it immediately that way, there would have been no reason to make any -- to put any question or to make any comment in that respect. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, as was the case with the witness yesterday, following the conclusion of their testimony, I am at this point going to be offering a number of contextual documents again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I must say I've had a personal hand in it and I find our house to be in order this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I take it that you have received them. Ms. Edgerton, would you please tell us what contextual documents you offered apart from the statements of the witness which have not yet been assigned an exhibit number as far as I remember because of the confusion in numbering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll deal first with the documents which have not previously been admitted as exhibits and then move to those which already have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will guide us through it. I wondered whether there would be any way of presenting these documents perhaps in the beginning of the testimony of a witness because if there is any relevant information in it which would raise any questions, it's too late now. And especially since they are presented as contextual but we'll consider that and perhaps Defence and Prosecution could think about whether they could come to a common view on that and the Chamber will think about it as well. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to the question of the exhibits, clearly these contextual documents that Ms. Edgerton has referred to, obviously I don't have objections to matters -- to documents and what have you that are already in evidence. But I'm going to need the opportunity to go through the other documents that have just been referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Therefore, the Chamber upon your request will reconsider whether this material should be admitted into evidence. We have now the problem the numbers are assigned so they are provisionally admitted. But we'll wait, let's say for the next 14 days, if there's any -- or if you would say I would need three weeks then.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well Your Honour perhaps a bit longer because I'm actually dealing with ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: All the witnesses this week and next so once I get out of court next week I can probably sit down and go through this lot of documents. So perhaps I think Your Honour's initial invitation for 14 days may be adequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then if we do not hear from you within the next 14 days, and let's then extend that -- that would be in the middle of the week we're not sitting. So let's say if not by Monday, the -- I think it's the 8th or the 9th, I'm not quite sure -- so if we will not hear by Monday in the first week after the short break, we have not heard from you, then the admission has become final and if we hear from you, we'll consider any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour. I think that does leave some outstanding matters in relation to not the last witness specifically but the previous two witnesses and that is that Ms. Edgerton and I need to come to some agreement about what aspect of the cross-examination can go back into open session in relation to 073. And I also think there's -- I've made two applications to strike evidence in relation to 073. So we still have those matters outstanding and they will have to be dealt with probably in the next two weeks we have in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the first matter the Chamber, of course, would like to hear the results of your conversations with Ms. Edgerton. On the second, we are working. We are working on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but with respect to these contextual documents there is an additional small number that I'd like to refer to on the record by their exhibit number which have previously been entered into exhibits, if I may, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so and do it slowly so that we get the correct numbers on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, is it -- can I go ahead or will you do it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are on the list -- yes. I have full confidence if in you, Ms. Edgerton, but in this respect, even more in Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Rightly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: While we're dealing with this, Your Honour, I would note that these documents are not necessarily specific to the witness who's just testified but relate to what would have been included in the Novo Sarajevo dossier, generally, they've already been selected for that dossier and in that sense are also relevant contextual documents for the witness who is to come tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what procedure is about to be adopted in relation to these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it is evidence that is already admitted and that Ms. Edgerton mainly wants to draw our attention that it is relevant for the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and that she specifically draws our attention to it in relation to the witness who testified today and yesterday and the witness who will testify tomorrow. So it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Procedurally, Your Honour, I'm just wondering is Madam Registrar about to read out the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, that's what I'm going to -- I write down in these documents, "Already in evidence as" and then Madam Registrar will tell us under what number they were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour. If those circumstances, I have an urgent matter to attend to. Can I just whilst Madam Registrar is reading out the numbers, can I just leave the court for two minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know whether you still find us when you are back, but please feel free to leave and I take it that you have no other matters to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Ms. Edgerton doesn't have any other matters to be raised, then I take it that you could copy the list and of course you are welcome to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be coming back. I have a very urgent matter to attend to right at this time and I will be back in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see you back. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now better understand that they were admitted but we had never yet received them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You're referring to yesterday's materials and I have in mind the materials not yet addressed for today which have already been admitted. I do need to refer to them on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go in the following order we see them. Telephone intercept 7 March 1992. So we didn't receive any copies on the documents you would like to put on the record. So I earlier expressed my confidence in you, Ms. Edgerton. Please proceed slowly reading the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To -- with respect to the contextual documents from Novo Sarajevo municipality, the Prosecution would also like to direct Your Honours's attention to exhibits which have been previously filed before the Trial Chamber and received the following numbers: The first being P529, tab 158 described as a report from Neskovic, president of Crisis Staff Novo Sarajevo to the president of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BiH dated 5 June 1992. That is an intercepted telephone conversation between Krajisnik Momcilo and Karadzic Radovan dated 1 January 1992, transcript and CD. The third presently has the number -- the numbers P67, that's 67, tab 30, and P292. And that's an intercepted telephone conversation between Krajisnik Momcilo, Koljevic Nikola, Ninkovic Radomir and Karasik Milenko dated 21 April 1992. The fourth is also bearing the number P292, and that's an intercepted telephone conversation between Vojislav Seselj and Branislav Gavrilovic dated 21 April 1992. The next presently bears the number P460 and 460A and 460A.1, being the numbers for the CD English transcript and B/C/S transcript. And that's an intercepted telephone conversation between Mandic Momcilo and Igor, also dated 21 April 1992. The last also bears the number P292. And it's an intercepted telephone conversation between Milenkovic and Krajisnik Momcilo also from 21 April 1992. Pardon me, I skipped over a note to myself. It's not the last, but it's the last but one. Finally, P273 and 273.1, 19 July 1992 being a letter to several Serbian municipalities signed by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just asking myself whether P292 has several tabs or KID numbers because we have got now only in this short series already three at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It has several tabs and I can -- and KID numbers, I see, on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you provide them to Madam Registrar who will then include them in the list to be -- no, this is just for the record, so they would not be on the list. If you would be so kind to provide to the Defence and to the Chamber this list and then adding the KID numbers so that what is on the record now is I think clear enough, could not lead to any confusion but just for our assistance, it would be helpful if it would have the tab or KID numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas, this is material that's already admitted into evidence and you get the further specifics from Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- and that was my confusion, we also have some contextual documents in relation to the last witness and since numbering now is no problem anymore, I'd like to ask Madam Registrar to guide us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there was some confusion about the numbering, Madam Registrar will start from the beginning from the last witness so that there would be no further confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for my orientation, what are the contextual documents, what numbers are they? Is it on from P600 upwards? Because, Ms. Loukas, these are the contextual documents on which you might want to further consider --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether or not to object.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do that in the same question, that they are provisionally admitted unless we hear from you until that same Monday that I just mentioned, that's the Monday after the week of non-sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that's the week commencing the 2nd of May, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The week we are not sitting is the week commencing the 2nd of May. As a matter of fact we are not sitting on from the -- I think from the 29th of April which is the birthday of the Dutch Queen.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, Queen's Day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to the intercepts contained in that range from CD 600, those were intercepts which, Your Honour, we had previously marked to be played to that witness, KRAJ 073. And taking into account there was no objection to the voice identification, move them into this category, if we can call that, of contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that objections against telephone conversation, especially if it's already clear that the identity of the interlocutors is not already in dispute might cause less problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other thing to be raised? If not, we'll adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom. Is that correct? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 20th day of April, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.19 p.m.
